item.title: Pelikani Taukei’aho on trial over fatal Wairarapa shooting
item.description: A Tongan man accused of murder is standing trial in the High Court at Wellington over a fatal shooting following an alleged drug deal in a Wairarapa supermarket car park. Pelikani Taukei’aho and co-defendant Tauave Sue have pleaded not guilty to the murder of Doreion Hard, who was fatally shot in Featherston on 22 March 2025.
item.content:encoded:
A Tongan man accused of murder is standing trial in the High Court at Wellington over a fatal shooting following an alleged drug deal in a Wairarapa supermarket car park.

Pelikani Taukei’aho and co-defendant Tauave Sue have pleaded not guilty to the murder of Doreion Hard, who was fatally shot in Featherston on 22 March 2025.

The Crown alleges the confrontation began after Hard and three other men arranged to meet the defendants to buy several ounces of cocaine, but instead planned to rob them.

Prosecutor Tim Bain has described the incident as a “drug deal gone sideways”.

The court heard the men arrived armed and that Hard and another man approached a grey Holden Cruze occupied by Taukei’aho and Sue.

A witness told the court the men appeared to rob the Holden’s occupants, with at least one allegedly brandishing a firearm while packages were removed from the vehicle.

The owner of a red ute used by Hard’s group testified that she heard a gunshot and saw the vehicle’s rear window shatter as they began leaving the car park.

She said Hard then grabbed her arm and told her he had been shot.

The woman told the jury she tried to stop Hard’s bleeding and keep him conscious while others in the ute were concerned with disposing of firearms and other items.

The Crown alleges Taukei’aho emerged from the Holden and fired at the departing ute, with one of the shots fatally striking Hard in the back.

Another witness, who told the court he had served in the military for 22 years, said he heard three or four shots during the rapidly unfolding incident.

Defence lawyers have questioned witnesses closely about the sequence and timing of events during the confrontation.

Hard was later found critically injured in Carterton and died despite emergency services attending.

Taukei’aho and Sue deny murder, and the allegations against them remain to be determined by the jury.

The trial has been allocated five weeks and is continuing.

item.title: Tongan graduate makes University of Auckland history with rare conjoint degree
item.description: A young New Zealand-born Tongan woman has become the first Pasifika student to graduate from the University of Auckland with a Bachelor of Commerce and Bachelor of Sport, Health and Physical Education conjoint degree. Meleana Payn, the youngest of five children and only daughter of Siliva and Joyce Payn, traces her Tongan roots to Mailetaha, Tongatapu, and Neiafu, Vavaʻu.
item.content:encoded:
A young New Zealand-born Tongan woman has become the first Pasifika student to graduate from the University of Auckland with a Bachelor of Commerce and Bachelor of Sport, Health and Physical Education conjoint degree.

Meleana Payn, the youngest of five children and only daughter of Siliva and Joyce Payn, traces her Tongan roots to Mailetaha, Tongatapu, and Neiafu, Vavaʻu.

Her graduation carries particular significance for her family, whose journey in New Zealand began when her maternal grandfather, Kapeliele Cocker, migrated from Tonga in the late 1960s seeking greater opportunities for his family.

“Everything I’ve been able to achieve is because of the sacrifices and opportunities he helped create for our family,” Payn said.

Education was strongly encouraged in her household, with Payn saying tertiary study was regarded as an expectation rather than simply an option.

She said her parents did not have the same educational opportunities while growing up in Tonga, making her achievement part of a family aspiration extending across generations.

Payn also credited Māori and Pacific support programmes at the university, including Tuākana Business and Commerce ‘o Pasifika and Pasifika Success within Sport, Health and Physical Education, for helping her succeed.

She said being surrounded by Pacific people provided strength and confidence and connected her with mentors who became role models and part of her university whānau.

Payn said that while she was honoured to be among the first Pasifika graduates completing the conjoint pathway, the greater significance was helping other Māori and Pacific students see themselves succeeding in higher education.

“What matters is creating pathways where our people can see themselves succeeding and feel confident enough to take up space in those places themselves,” she said.

Her academic journey is continuing, with Payn now studying a Master of Business in Sport Leadership and Management at Auckland University of Technology.

Influenced by her father’s involvement in rugby in Tonga and New Zealand, her research interests centre on increasing opportunities for Pacific people in sport leadership and management.

Alongside her postgraduate studies, Payn is Tuākana Business Head Tutor Pacific, a role through which she hopes to provide other Māori and Pacific students with the support she received during her own studies.

For Payn, the graduation belongs not only to her but to the family and community that supported her.

“I owe it all to my village,” she said. “This is a huge win for all of us. But I also know the job’s not finished.”
